transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

For the last few weeks I’ve just been on this intense high, like I’m wired all the time and can’t turn it off, and it’s starting to scare people at work. It actually got so bad today that I was escorted out of the office, and my manager and coworker convinced me I needed to come to the emergency department.
Before this current high-energy period, have you ever had a past episode of depression or a similar high/overactive episode? If so, were you ever diagnosed with bipolar disorder?

Yeah, looking back, I've had periods of really low moods and other times where I felt revved-up like this, though I never heard any voices during those past times. But no, I've never been formally diagnosed with bipolar disorder before this current crisis.

During this current high-energy episode, have you been hearing or seeing things other people don’t, or strongly believing things that others say aren’t true? If yes, did those experiences happen only while your mood was unusually high?

Yes, lately I've been hearing a deep male voice right behind my left ear telling me things like "You were chosen for this," which turns harsh and critical when I start to doubt myself. This only started once I hit this intense high around the project launch, and I've never experienced anything like it during my past low moods or normal times.

There is also clear psychotic symptomatology during the current elevated episode (hearing a voice and grandiose content), which makes the non-psychotic elevated-episode candidate F31.1 less likely. The psychotic experiences appear confined to the current elevated state, so the current leading candidate is F31.2.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a current manic/high-energy episode lasting several weeks with clear functional impairment requiring removal from work, along with mood-congruent psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations and grandiose/paranoid-type beliefs) occurring only during the elevated mood state. The history of prior depressive and revved-up episodes supports bipolar disorder rather than an isolated psychotic or single manic disorder.
